paper.cite: Szymanski, M. D., Bain, D. E., Kiehl, K., Pennington, S., Wong, S., & Henry, K. R. (1999). Killer whale (Orcinus orca) hearing: Auditory brainstem response and behavioral audiograms. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 106(2), 1134–1141.

lede: Before the prisons and the mobile MRI, there were whales. Early in his career, in the 1990s, Kent Kiehl worked with Michael Szymanski, David Bain and colleagues at the University of California, Davis and the Marine World Foundation on a question that sounds simple and is not: can you record the electrical activity of a killer whale's brain from the outside of its head, while the animal is awake, calm and free to swim away?

The answer was yes. The team recorded auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), the tiny volleys of electrical activity that travel from the ear through the brainstem in the first hundredth of a second after a sound, from two adult female killer whales named Yaka and Vigga. The study was published in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America in 1999.

sections: How do you record a brainwave from a killer whale?

The recordings were made at Marine World Africa USA, an oceanarium in Vallejo, California, in 1995 and 1996, in a sea-water pool about 15 meters across. Each whale was trained to hold still beside the pool wall with her head against a target and her blowhole above the surface.

A trainer then placed two gold EEG electrodes, each set inside a suction cup, on the whale's skin: one about 17 cm behind the blowhole and one further back toward the dorsal fin. An underwater speaker a meter in front of her played very brief tone bursts, 30 per second. The signal between the two electrodes was amplified 100,000 times, and the responses to 350 tone bursts were averaged to pull the brainstem response out of the background. Each pair of recordings took two to three minutes, after which the suction cups came off, the whale was rewarded with fish, and she swam off before coming back for the next one.

The team lowered the volume step by step until the response disappeared, and repeated this at twelve frequencies from 1 to 100 kHz. The same two whales had earlier been tested behaviorally, trained to respond when they heard a tone, so the two ways of measuring hearing could be compared directly in the same animals. That had not been reported before in a whale or dolphin.

Killer whales hear best at about 20 kHz, lower than most other toothed whales and dolphins, but right where the energy of their own echolocation clicks is concentrated. Both whales heard tones up to 100 kHz and one responded at 120 kHz. An earlier study of a single young male had put the upper limit at 32 kHz, so the new result substantially changed the picture of what killer whales can hear.

Thresholds read from the brainstem response followed the same curve as the behavioral thresholds and were, on average, 12 dB less sensitive; in the whales' best range (18–42 kHz) the two agreed to within about 5 dB. In other words, a few minutes of brain recording gives a useful estimate of what a whale can hear, without the months of training a behavioral hearing test requires.

The responses were also very small, at most about a millionth of a volt, roughly ten times smaller than in dolphins. The authors attributed this to body size: a killer whale's brain is a much smaller fraction of its body than a dolphin's, and they predicted that the method would be harder still in the great baleen whales.

Knowing what whales can hear is the starting point for judging how shipping, sonar and construction noise affect them. The 1999 audiograms have been used as reference data for killer whale hearing in the years since, and evoked-potential hearing tests are now a routine tool for stranded and rehabilitated whales and dolphins.
To our knowledge, an adult killer whale remains the largest animal from which auditory brainstem responses and a full brain-based audiogram have been recorded.

The brainstem response is only the first hundredth of a second of what a brain does with a sound. The later, larger brain potentials that the Kiehl Lab uses every day to study attention, memory and language in people have barely been explored in whales. Do killer whales show the brain's signature of noticing something unexpected? Does a familiar call from their own pod register differently from a stranger's?

Recording technology has changed enormously since the 1990s. Amplifiers that once filled an equipment rack now fit inside a suction cup, and many channels can be recorded at once and sent wirelessly to a laptop on the pool deck. The lab would like to build a portable multi-channel EEG system for cetaceans and return to these questions with animals in human care.

Behavioral thresholds are RMS levels and brainstem (ABR) thresholds are peak-to-peak levels, both in dB re 1 µPa; behavioral thresholds were not reported at 1 and 2 kHz.
